subject: biology
title: Measuring energy in food (calorimetry)
key_idea: The energy in food can be measured by burning a sample under a container of water. The energy released heats the water. The temperature rise and the mass of water give the energy in joules.

blocks.text: A calorimeter transfers the energy released when food burns to a known mass of water. This section covers the apparatus and what each part does.

rows: Releases heat energy, which heats the water
Absorbs the energy. The mass of water is known.
Measures the start and end temperature of the water
Spreads the heat evenly, so all the water is at the same temperature
Acts as an insulator. It reduces heat loss and stops water evaporating.

blocks.text: A bomb calorimeter works in the same way. The food sample is burnt and the temperature rise of the water is measured.

items: Energy from the burning food heats the water.
A lid reduces heat loss. A stirrer makes the temperature even.
A bigger temperature rise means more energy was released.

blocks.text: Follow the steps in order. The same steps are used for every food so that the foods can be compared.

diagram.alt: Put the stages of the calorimetry investigation in order.
diagram.prompt: Put the calorimetry method in order
steps: Measure the mass of the food sample
Measure a known mass of water into the calorimeter and record its start temperature
Burn the food so that it heats the water, stirring the water
Record the final temperature of the water
Subtract the start temperature from the final temperature

items: Use the same mass or volume of water each time.
Use the same mass of food.
Keep the burning food the same distance from the calorimeter.
Use the same starting temperature of water.
Make sure the food is burnt completely.
Repeat with each food.
Measure the temperature before and after. The temperature change is the final temperature minus the start temperature.
Control the mass of water, the mass of food and the distance from the flame.
Burn the food completely.

blocks.text: Use the temperature change and the mass of water to find the energy in joules.

blocks.label: Energy transferred to the water
blocks.formula: energy = mass of water × 4.2 × temperature change
where: 4.2 is the energy needed to heat 1 g of water by 1 °C, in J

items.text: A piece of cheese heats 25 g of water from 21 °C to 85 °C. The change is 85 − 21 = 64 °C.

diagram.alt: Practise calculating the energy in food from the mass of water and the temperature change.
diagram.question: A food sample heats **{m} g** of water by **{t} °C**. Calculate the energy transferred to the water in joules, using energy = mass of water × 4.2 × temperature change.
working: Energy = mass of water × 4.2 × temperature change

blocks.label: Energy per gram of food
blocks.formula: energy per gram = energy transferred ÷ mass of food
where: mass of food burnt, in g

items: Use the temperature change, not the final temperature.
Energy = mass of water × 4.2 × temperature change.
Divide by the mass of food burnt to compare foods.

blocks.text: Exam questions ask why two foods or two results are different.

items: Foods with more fat have more energy. Avocado has more energy than apple because it contains more fat.
A smaller temperature rise means less energy was transferred to the water.
Reasons for less energy transferred: the food contained less energy or fat, a smaller mass of food burned, or the food was held further away from the container.
Heat lost to the surroundings means the measured energy is lower than the real energy in the food.
Use comparative words such as more, less, higher and lower.
Link a smaller temperature change to less energy transferred.

checks.q: Give one function of the lid on a calorimeter.
checks.a: It stops heat loss or evaporation of water.

checks.q: Why is the water in the calorimeter stirred?
checks.a: To make sure the heat is distributed evenly, so that all the water is at the same temperature.

checks.q: A food heats 50 g of water by 30 °C. Calculate the energy content of the food.

exam_phrases: use the thermometer to measure the start and end temperature of the water
subtract the initial temperature from the final temperature
it is an insulator / reduces heat loss
stops heat loss / evaporation of water
ensures heat is distributed evenly throughout the water
use the same mass / volume of water, the same mass of food
less energy was transferred to the water

mistakes.right: Use the temperature change, 85 − 21 = 64 °C. Energy = 25 × 4.2 × 64 = 6720 J. One mark is given for a correct calculation from an incorrect temperature change.

mistakes.wrong: The temperature rise is found by measuring the difference.
mistakes.right: "Measure the difference" is ignored. Say measure the start and end temperature with a thermometer, then calculate the difference.

mistakes.wrong: The lid stops unwanted substances getting in.
mistakes.right: This is ignored. The lid stops heat loss, or evaporation of water.

mistakes.wrong: Avocado has 669 kJ and apple has 220 kJ.
mistakes.right: Stated values and differences are ignored unless they are comparative. Say avocado has more energy than apple because it contains more fat.

worked_example.question:
A calorimeter was used to measure the energy content of a piece of cheese.

The mass of water was 25 g. The starting temperature of the water was 21 °C and the final temperature of the water was 85 °C.

Calculate the energy content of this piece of cheese.

Use the equation

energy in joules (J) = mass of water × 4.2 × temperature change
worked_example.tip: Full marks for the correct answer without working. One mark for a correct calculation from an incorrect temperature change.
